title: Area XII review: Emergency Operations
intro: These questions mix the four Tasks of Area XII: emergency descent, emergency approach and landing, systems and equipment malfunctions, and emergency equipment and survival gear, from the instructor's seat. Many join two of them in one flight, such as an engine fire that becomes a forced landing, a static blockage found in an emergency descent, a firm landing after a simulated forced landing that sets off the ELT, or an engine failure over a lake where best glide and a nearby boat decide the plan.

questions.q: Your learner calls a simulated engine fire at 6,500 ft AGL in a fixed-gear single, calls out mixture idle cutoff and fuel selector off, and rolls into the descent. He says, 'I will hold the top of the yellow arc all the way down, because the faster we go, the sooner the fire blows out.' What do you teach?
options: Good plan: the AFH aim is to get down as rapidly as possible, and a high airspeed is the one method it lists for putting out an engine fire, so speed comes ahead of any structural concerns
Speed might blow the fire out, but a weakened structure argues for a slower descent, a fire that seems out can rekindle as the speed changes, and this ends in a forced landing
Slow to best glide at once and stay level until the fire is out, because the AFH says not to descend while a fire may still be burning under the cowling
Keep the high speed until the flames are gone, then restart the engine so there is power to stretch the descent all the way to the nearest airport
questions.why: In an engine fire a high airspeed descent could blow out the fire, but the weakening of the structure is a major concern and a descent at low airspeed places less stress on the airplane [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. Fires that appear to be out have been known to rekindle with changes in airflow pattern and airspeed, and a powerless single has no choice but a forced landing [[24:359|AFH 18-10]], so the descent is also the time to choose the field. Once the flames are out, no restart should be attempted [[24:358|AFH 18-9]], which rules out the restart plan. Nothing says to stay level: the airplane is expendable and only the people aboard matter [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

questions.q: In the debrief your learner says, 'I start every level-off 100 feet early, since the ACS gives me plus or minus 100 feet.' Today she came down at 1,800 fpm to a specified 4,000 ft MSL and finished at 3,870 ft. What do you tell her?
options: She finished 130 ft low, outside the tolerance; the IFH lead is 10 percent of the descent rate, here about 180 ft, so start near 4,180 ft, and the 100 feet is the finish tolerance, not a lead
Her habit is right and she was inside the tolerance: the 100 feet is counted from the altitude where she began the level-off, which today was 4,100 ft
Her habit fails only at high rates: above 1,000 fpm the IFH lead becomes 20 percent of the descent rate, so she should have started near 4,360 ft
Her habit is right; the 130-foot miss came from a pull that was too slow, so next time she should snap the nose up firmly as she passes 4,100 ft
questions.why: The ±100 feet is measured from the specified level-off altitude (CFI ACS AI.XII.A.S5): 4,000 - 3,870 = 130 ft, so she was out. The IFH leads a level-off by an altitude equal to 10 percent of the rate of descent [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]: 0.10 x 1,800 = 180 ft, so start about 4,180 ft; a 100 ft lead is late at this rate. A late pitch change tends to overshoot unless it is made rapidly, and rapid changes can lead to control issues or spatial disorientation [[23:211|IFH 7-50]], so snapping the nose up is the wrong fix. The IFH gives one rule, 10 percent, with no larger figure for high rates.

questions.q: Simulated cabin smoke at 7,500 ft in thick haze with no clear horizon. Your learner snaps the throttle to idle and, instead of rolling into the bank, raises the nose, saying it felt as if the airplane had pitched down. What is happening, and what do you teach?
options: A somatogravic illusion: a quick throttle reduction can lead a disoriented pilot to pull into a nose-up or stall attitude; cross-check the attitude indicator, not the feeling, and set the 30 to 45 degree bank

The Coriolis illusion: reaching for the throttle moved her head, so the fix is to hold her head still, keep the nose up where she put it and wait until the pitching feeling has faded away before she rolls into any bank
An inversion illusion from the power change; the fix is to push the nose well down at once so the airplane matches the feeling of tumbling backward
Nothing to fix: a nose-up pause after closing the throttle is how the AFH bleeds off speed before the bank, so she should hold it until the stall warning sounds
questions.why: A rapid deceleration by quick reduction of the throttle can lead the disoriented pilot to pull the aircraft into a nose-up or stall attitude, the opposite of the nose-up feeling a rapid acceleration gives: the somatogravic illusion [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. Without good visual references the instruments, not the inner ear, must win. The Coriolis illusion follows a head movement after a long turn, and the inversion illusion comes from an abrupt change from climb to level flight [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. The AFH entry is a bank of about 30 to 45 degrees to keep the load factor positive, with no nose-up pause [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

questions.q: To save time on a cool, damp morning, you plan one long exercise in a carbureted single: a simulated engine fire at 8,500 ft, the emergency descent at idle all the way down, then straight into a simulated forced landing to a field, still at idle. What do the sources say about the engine?
options: The plan is sound: a forced landing follows an engine fire anyway, and a long idle descent from 8,500 ft keeps the cylinders warm and even, so the engine takes full power at once when you call terminate at the bottom, with no clearing needed

Split it: end the descent once it is stable, since prolonged practice overcools the cylinders and fast descents can shock cool them; for the glide, carb heat on before the throttle closes, and keep the engine warm and cleared
The plan is sound if the learner leans the mixture during the idle, because the AFH keeps the engine warm in emergency descents by leaning rather than by using the throttle
Split it only to cut the workload: a long idle descent does nothing to the engine, but flying both maneuvers in one exercise is too much for a learner to manage at once
questions.why: When the descent is established and stabilized in training it should be terminated, and prolonged practice of emergency descents should be avoided to prevent excessive cooling of the cylinders [[24:358|AFH 18-9]]. High-speed descents can also shock cool the engine with abrupt temperature changes [[1:177|PHAK 7-17]]. For the glide, keep the engine warm and cleared during all simulated emergency landings [[24:200|AFH 9-29]], and if carburetor icing is suspected put the heat full on before closing the throttle and open the throttle for a few seconds now and then [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]. No source keeps the engine warm by leaning.

questions.q: You are about to roll into a practice emergency descent when 121.5 MHz carries a synthesized voice announcing 'pilot incapacitation' and a diversion, and you spot a small single descending ahead toward the airport you would have used as your landing field. What should you do?
options: Call the aircraft on 121.5 MHz and agree on separation with it, because an Emergency Autoland system answers calls from ATC and from other pilots once its first broadcast is done and over
Carry on with the descent as planned: Emergency Autoland uses ADS-B and its terrain database to steer around other traffic, so the conflict is its problem
Hold off the practice and stay out of its path: an Emergency Autoland system takes no evasive action, cannot detect and avoid other aircraft, and does not react to ATC instructions
Descend quickly below it and continue, because Emergency Autoland stays above 12,000 ft MSL until its one-minute-out call to the runway
questions.why: EAL systems currently take no evasive action against another aircraft, although they transmit on the radio, and pilots should avoid the path of any aircraft under EAL control or suspected to be [[24:33|AFH 1-12]]. They cannot detect and avoid traffic or receive or react to ATC instructions [[24:372|AFH 18-23]], and controllers are told to assume transmissions to the aircraft will not be acknowledged [[34:340|AIM PCG E-1]]. ADS-B is how it reports its own position, and the terrain database is for obstacles; 12 miles and 12,000 ft MSL is where it starts broadcasting on tower or CTAF [[24:371|AFH 18-22]]. An emergency descent drops through other traffic, so clearing comes first [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

questions.q: Another instructor tells your learner, 'The AFH says every simulated engine failure in a single ends at 500 feet AGL.' What do the sources in this Area actually give for ending a simulated emergency landing?
options: That figure is right: the AFH sets 500 feet AGL as the termination point for single-engine airplanes, with a go-around flown from that altitude
1,500 feet AGL: the AFH ends simulated emergency landings at the same floor it gives for recovering from practice stalls in single-engine airplanes, so the go-around starts there
1,000 feet AGL: the AFH ends the simulation at the key position, at normal traffic pattern altitude, before the power-off approach begins
No altitude: end it as soon as you can tell whether a safe landing is assured, and never go on to where it causes undue hazard or annoyance to people or property below
questions.why: The AFH says every simulated emergency landing approach is terminated as soon as it can be determined whether a safe landing is assured, and never continued to a point that creates an undue hazard or an annoyance to persons or property on the ground [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]. No source gives a termination altitude for a single. The 1,500 feet AGL figure is for stall recovery practice [[24:121|AFH 5-16]], and the key position at pattern altitude is where the normal power-off approach starts, not where the simulation ends [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]. On the checkride the evaluator gives a simulated failure only where a safe landing could be completed (CFI ACS Appendix 2).

questions.q: A real engine failure at 4,000 ft AGL in a low-wing trainer whose fuel selector has only LEFT and RIGHT. After setting best glide, your learner sees the selector on LEFT, the left gauge at a quarter and the right at half. She says, 'The left tank has fuel, so fuel is not the problem,' and moves on to the magnetos. What do you tell her?
options: Good order: when the gauge shows fuel, the AFH says to leave the selector alone, so a restart is not starved by switching to a tank full of air
Switch to the right tank anyway: many forced landings came from a selector on an empty tank while the other held plenty, and fuel gauges can be inaccurate
Skip the fuel items and go straight to the forced landing checklist, because restart attempts at 4,000 ft AGL use up the altitude she needs for the field
Switch tanks only if the electric fuel pump fails to bring the power back first, since the AFH lists the fuel pump ahead of the selector
questions.why: The critical items include the fuel selector position and the quantity in the selected tank. Many actual emergency landings were later traced to a selector on an empty tank while the other tank had plenty of fuel, and it may be wise to change tanks even though the gauge shows fuel, because fuel gauges can be inaccurate [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]. The habit the AFH wants is checking these items while choosing a field and planning the approach, not instead of it [[24:200|AFH 9-29]], so skipping them is wrong. The AFH lists the selector first, before the fuel pressure gauge.

questions.q: After a real engine fire at 5,500 ft, fuel off and the flames out, your learner glides toward a field in a trainer with electric flaps. Your POH fire procedure does not mention the master switch, but she reaches for it: 'Master off, it was a fire.' What do you say?
options: Leave it on for now: the fire was not electrical and no crash landing is imminent, so it keeps the radios and transponder; switch it off before touchdown, once the flaps are set
Switch it off now: the AFH treats every fire as electrical until proven otherwise, and the radios do nothing useful once the field has been chosen
Leave it on all the way through the touchdown and the stop, because the AFH says shutting down the electrical system before touchdown makes a post-crash fire more likely, so keep it on until stopped
Switch it off now and back on only for the flaps on short final, because the AFH says to cycle the master before landing to find any faulty circuit
questions.why: Unless the fire is electrical or a crash landing is imminent, turning off the electrical system prevents the use of panel radios for distress calls and makes ATC lose the transponder return [[24:358|AFH 18-9]]. Before touchdown, deactivating the electrical system reduces the likelihood of a post-crash fire, but the battery master should not go off until the pilot no longer needs electrical power for vital systems [[24:353|AFH 18-4]], here the electric flaps. Cycling the master and switches one at a time is for an electrical fire when power is essential, and it recreates the problem [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

questions.q: Your learner's forced landing field can be used in either direction, with a 15-knot wind straight along it. He plans to touch down at 55 knots and, to save a turn, wants to land downwind. Compared with landing into the wind, about how much more destructive energy would that touchdown carry?
options: About 1.75 times: groundspeed goes from 40 to 70 knots, and the destructive energy grows in step with it
About the same: the touchdown airspeed is 55 knots in both directions, and airspeed is what sets the energy
About 9 times: the destructive energy grows with the cube of groundspeed, so a little more speed costs a lot
About 3 times: groundspeed goes from 40 to 70 knots, and the energy grows with the square of groundspeed
questions.why: Groundspeed is the most critical factor in the severity of the stop: doubling it quadruples the destructive energy, so energy grows with its square, and touchdown should be at the lowest controllable airspeed [[24:352|AFH 18-3]]. Downwind: 55 + 15 = 70 knots; into the wind: 55 - 15 = 40 knots. (70 / 40)^2 = 1.75^2 = 3.06, about 3 times. The 1.75 answer forgets the square. A tailwind helps the glide reach a field [[24:84|AFH 3-23]], but not the touchdown.

questions.q: You give a simulated failure at 2,500 ft AGL over forest with a few small clearings. Your learner turns toward a smooth hayfield well beyond gliding range, the nose creeping up and the airspeed 15 knots below best glide. What is the error, and what do you teach?
options: Eagerness to get down: she should lower the nose further and dive toward the hayfield, so that the extra airspeed carries her the rest of the way there

A sound choice badly flown: the hayfield is the only safe option in sight, and slowing below best glide adds distance when a field is just out of reach, so she should hold the slower speed all the way there and then land on it

The desire to save the airplane: she is stretching the glide toward a nicer field. Back to best glide and the best spot within reach; a well-flown crash landing in poor terrain can beat an uncontrolled one on a good field
Undue concern about getting hurt: reassure her and let her keep the slower speed, since minimum sink keeps the airplane in the air the longest
questions.why: A pilot conditioned in training to always find a safe field when the throttle closes may stretch the glide to reach a more appealing field, the desire to save the airplane [[24:351|AFH 18-2]]. The cardinal rule is never to stretch a glide below best glide; it lands short and can stall [[24:84|AFH 3-23]], and 15 knots slow is also outside the ±10 knots of CFI ACS AI.XII.B.S1. A well-executed crash landing in poor terrain can be less hazardous than an uncontrolled touchdown on an established field [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]. Minimum sink buys time, not distance [[24:84|AFH 3-23]], and diving at a field is the opposite fault [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

questions.q: The engine quits at 3,000 ft over a large lake in a trainer with an 8 to 1 glide ratio. A ferry is 3.5 NM ahead, and the shore is far out of reach. Your learner sets minimum sink speed 'because the AFH says to use it for ditching.' What do you teach?
options: Fly best glide: it reaches about 3.9 NM in still air, so the ferry is in range, while minimum sink buys time but covers less distance, and the AIM says to ditch near a surface vessel
She is right: minimum sink is the slower speed, so it covers the most distance over the water and also gives the most time for the MAYDAY call
Fly a little below minimum sink to stretch the glide, since at 3.5 NM the ferry sits near the edge of the still-air range and every foot counts
Ditch at once near the present position, because the AIM says to stay well away from boats, whose wake could swamp a ditched airplane
questions.why: Glide ratio is distance traveled for altitude lost; 10,000 ft forward for 1,000 ft down is 10 to 1 [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]. Here 3,000 x 8 = 24,000 ft, and 24,000 / 6,076 = 3.95 NM, so best glide reaches the ferry in still air. Minimum sink keeps the airplane up longest but at a lower speed and over less distance; the AFH gives ditching at sea as an example of when time matters more than distance [[24:84|AFH 3-23]], but here distance to a vessel matters, because the AIM says to make every effort to ditch near a surface vessel [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]]. Never stretch a glide below best glide [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

questions.q: On the ground you brief an engine fire scenario for your constant-speed single. Your learner's plan is mixture idle cutoff, fuel selector off, ignition off, then an emergency descent with the propeller full forward. You add that the smoke in this scenario is thick and black. What does the AFH say to change, unless the POH says otherwise?
options: Nothing changes: thick black smoke marks a fuel-fed fire, so shutting off the fuel already removes everything that is feeding it, and the ignition may go off as planned to stop the engine at once
Turn the fuel back on: thick black smoke means the fire is fed by oil, so the fuel shutoff does nothing, and a restart will blow the smoke clear
Leave the ignition on to burn the fuel in the lines; thick black smoke points to an oil-fed fire, so consider stopping the propeller, pitch control at minimum rpm and the nose up to slow
Keep the propeller at high rpm and add speed, because the engine-driven oil pump stops feeding the fire only when the airspeed is high enough
questions.why: Unless the AFM/POH directs otherwise, the first step is mixture to idle cutoff and fuel selector off, with the ignition left on to use up the fuel in the lines; if the flames go out, no restart. If the fire is oil-fed, shown by thick black smoke rather than the bright orange flames of a fuel fire, the pilot should consider stopping the propeller, with a constant-speed propeller by setting minimum rpm and raising the nose to slow until it stops, so the engine-driven pump stops feeding the fire [[24:358|AFH 18-9]]. A powerless single then makes a forced landing [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

questions.q: In a retractable single, the main gear shows down and locked, but the nose gear will not extend by the normal or the alternate method in the POH. You have two hours of fuel. Which plan fits the AFH?
options: The nearest rough grass strip, since a hard runway surface makes sparks; then hold full up-elevator against the stop through the rollout so the nose stays up as long as it possibly can before it touches the surface
Any runway at all, with full fuel to keep the weight forward, then firm braking right away to cut the time the nose is unsupported and get the airplane stopped
Raise the mains and land with all three up, because the AFH calls a gear-up landing the only safe choice whenever any one gear leg fails to extend

An airport with crash and rescue and equipment standing by, fuel burned off if practical; on the mains, hold the nose off until nearly full up-elevator, then ease off so it settles slowly, braking only if needed
questions.why: When a gear leg will not respond to the normal or alternate extension, the pilot should pick an airport with crash and rescue facilities, ask for emergency equipment to stand by, and consider burning off fuel to cut landing speed and fire potential; a smooth hard runway usually causes less damage than a rough grass strip, though it can make sparks [[24:361|AFH 18-12]]. With the nose wheel retracted and the mains down, hold the nose off until almost full up-elevator, then release back pressure so the nose settles slowly; holding full up-elevator lets it drop abruptly, and brakes are used only if absolutely necessary to avoid obstacles [[24:361|AFH 18-12]] [[24:362|AFH 18-13]]. Landing with all gear up is an option for one failed main leg, not a rule [[24:361|AFH 18-12]].

questions.q: Your learner selects flaps on downwind, and the airplane rolls hard to the right; she holds it with almost full left aileron and a lot of right rudder. Two runways are open, one with a 10-knot crosswind from the left and one with the same crosswind from the right. Which plan fits the AFH?
options: The left flap is down: use the runway with the crosswind from the right, fly the approach faster than normal and fly it onto the runway instead of flaring hard
The right flap is down: use the runway with the crosswind from the left, fly the approach slower than normal and flare fully so it touches down as slowly as possible
The left flap is down: use the runway with the crosswind from the left, because that crosswind lifts the low wing and cuts the aileron she needs to hold it
Either runway will do: a split flap needs only aileron, so fly a normal approach speed and flare, and choose the runway that gives the shorter taxi back
questions.why: A split flap shows as a pronounced roll toward the wing with the least flap deflection, so a roll to the right means the left flap is out. It is held with opposite aileron and substantial opposite rudder, a cross-controlled condition, and almost full aileron may be needed. The pilot should not land with a crosswind from the side of the deployed flap, because the extra roll control may not be there, so take the crosswind from the right. Fly the approach faster than normal and fly it onto the runway at a safe margin above flaps-up stall speed rather than flaring excessively [[24:360|AFH 18-11]].

questions.q: Day VFR in a fixed-gear trainer with electric flaps, the alternator fails and will not reset, and your learner sheds load. The nearest airport has a 2,400 ft runway; one 10 NM farther has 4,000 ft. Today's POH landing distance with flaps is 1,700 ft. Which plan fits the sources?
options: The 2,400 ft runway, waiting to select the flaps on short final, after the battery has had time to rest, so that the landing distance stays at the normal 1,700 ft
Plan a no-flap landing on the 4,000 ft runway: without flaps it could need as much as 50 percent more, about 2,550 ft, and selecting the flap motor on a weak battery could cut all power
The 2,400 ft runway with no flaps, because a no-flap landing adds at most 10 percent, about 1,870 ft, which leaves plenty of runway to spare
Continue to the destination 35 minutes away, since the IFH gives about 40 minutes of battery life, enough to finish the trip with power left over
questions.why: Electrically operated flaps may not work on a partly depleted battery, and selecting their motors may cause an immediate total loss of electrical power, so plan the arrival early and expect a no-flap landing [[24:362|AFH 18-13]] [[24:363|AFH 18-14]]. A no-flap landing needs substantially more runway, as much as 50 percent more [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]: 1,700 x 1.5 = 2,550 ft, more than 2,400 ft. The IFH's 40 minutes is an approximation not to be relied on, and a pilot should never continue once the charging system has failed but land at the nearest suitable airport [[23:330|IFH 11-5]]; a runway shorter than the no-flap distance is not suitable.

questions.q: IFR at 7,000 ft, cabin smoke forces your learner to start down before she can get a clearance. Safely on the ground, she says, 'Now I am in trouble, or at least I owe the FAA a report.' What is accurate?
options: The deviation was lawful only because she said MAYDAY first, since 91.3 lets a pilot leave a clearance only once an emergency has been declared on the frequency

She must send a written report of the deviation to the FAA within 10 days in every case, whether or not anyone asks for it, and she also had to declare an emergency on the frequency before she left her assigned altitude

Neither is automatic: 91.3 let her deviate as far as the emergency required, a written report is due only if the Administrator asks, and her duty was to tell ATC as soon as possible and get an amended clearance
Nothing more was required: a deviation under 91.3 carries no duty to tell ATC about it and no duty to report it to anyone after the landing
questions.why: In an in-flight emergency requiring immediate action, the PIC may deviate from any part 91 rule to the extent required, and a PIC who deviates shall, upon the request of the Administrator, send a written report [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3]]. A pilot who uses that authority to deviate from an ATC clearance must notify ATC as soon as possible and obtain an amended clearance [[34:28|AIM 6-1-1]]. 91.3 sets no 10-day report and does not require a declaration first, although declaring an emergency brings extra help and priority handling [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].

questions.q: In a practice emergency descent your learner has the same idle power, configuration and pitch as always, yet the airspeed reads 8 knots over her ceiling, the VSI shows about half the usual rate and the altimeter unwinds slowly. She starts raising the nose to get the airspeed back. What do you suspect, and what is the check?
options: A pitot tube blocked with its drain hole open; the check is to watch whether the airspeed falls to zero once she has leveled off and everything has settled
A partial static blockage, which makes the airplane look too high, too fast and slow to descend; open the alternate static source now, while descending, and use it if the needles jump
A partial static blockage; open the alternate static source only after the level-off, because a valid comparison of the needles needs them steady in level flight, not moving in a descent
Nothing is wrong: fast descents always make the VSI and altimeter lag behind, so she should keep raising the nose until the airspeed comes back
questions.why: Partial static blockage may show nothing until a descent; then the altimeter reads higher than actual, the VSI shows less descent than actual, and the airspeed indicator reads higher than actual, so the instruments say too high, too fast and descending much slower than desired [[24:363|AFH 18-14]] [[24:364|AFH 18-15]]. Confirm it by opening the alternate static source while climbing or descending; if the needles move significantly, use it for the rest of the flight [[24:364|AFH 18-15]]. A blocked pitot with the drain open makes the airspeed drop to zero, not read high [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].

questions.q: A rough-running engine leads your learner to a good precautionary landing in a remote pasture. No one is hurt, the radio reaches no one, there is no flight plan, and the airplane has a 121.5 MHz ELT. She says, 'The ELT will bring a satellite fix within minutes.' What do you correct?
options: Nothing: the satellites still pick up 121.5 MHz signals and pass a position to the rescuers, so staying in place for a few minutes is all that she needs to do
The ELT can only start from crash forces, so after a gentle landing it cannot help at all, and she should walk out to look for help before it gets dark
A 121.5 MHz ELT runs for only about 12 hours, so she should leave it off until she hears an airplane overhead, then switch it on to save the battery

Satellites stopped listening on 121.5 MHz in 2009, so the signal needs a nearby ATC facility or an overflying aircraft, and with no flight plan about 36 hours normally pass before family concern starts an alert; switch it on by hand, verify it, and stay with the airplane
questions.why: Cospas-Sarsat stopped monitoring 121.5 and 243.0 MHz in 2009, so analog ELTs depend on a nearby ATC facility or an overflying aircraft; ELTs run at least 48 hours, and pilots and passengers should know how to activate one by hand and verify it is transmitting [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]]. SAR forces normally wait for confirmation, such as an overdue report, before acting on an analog alert, which can take hours [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]]. Without a flight plan, 36 hours normally pass before family concern starts an alert [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]]. After a crash landing, unless you have good reason to think you will not be found, remain with the aircraft and prepare signals [[34:47|AIM 6-3-2]].

questions.q: Your private pilot learner plans a personal flight, not for hire, in a single across a lake 30 NM wide, well beyond power-off gliding distance from shore. He says, '91.205 makes me carry a vest for everyone and a flare.' What do you teach?
options: He is right: 91.205(b)(12) requires flotation gear for each occupant and a pyrotechnic signaling device on any flight beyond power-off gliding distance from shore
He needs even more: 91.509 requires liferafts and a portable survival radio for any airplane flying more than 30 minutes or 100 NM from the nearest shore
Nothing to teach: with no rule for his flight, a bulky foam PFD stowed under each seat meets the AIM advice just as well as an inflatable vest would
91.205(b)(12) applies only when the aircraft is operated for hire, so here the gear is his decision; the AIM points to inflatable vests worn uninflated, inflated after exiting, with everyone briefed
questions.why: 91.205(b)(12) requires approved flotation gear for each occupant and at least one pyrotechnic signaling device only if the aircraft is operated for hire over water beyond power-off gliding distance from shore [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(12)]]. 91.509 sits in subpart F, which governs large airplanes, turbojet-powered airplanes with more than one engine and fractional ownership aircraft, not a light single [[60:527|14 CFR 91.501(a)]] [[60:531|14 CFR 91.509(b)]]. Survival after a forced landing at sea depends on proficiency and effective water survival gear [[34:35|AIM 6-2-6]]. FAA-approved inflatable vests are worn uninflated and inflated after exiting; bulky PFDs can block narrow exits, and passengers must be briefed on them [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9]].

questions.q: Your learner files one VFR flight plan for a three-leg trip with stops, ETA at the final destination 1645. His planned arrival at the first stop is 1000. If he goes down on the first leg at 0940 and no other information reaches anyone, about when would the search probably start, and how much sooner had he filed only to the first stop?
options: About 1645, at the final ETA; a plan filed only to the first stop would have started it at 1000, about 6 hours 45 minutes sooner
About 1030 either way, because Flight Service starts a search 30 minutes after the ETA at each stop listed on one flight plan
About 1715; a plan filed only to the first stop would have started it at about 1030, about 6 hours 45 minutes sooner
About 36 hours after 0940 either way, because a flight plan matters only once family concern has started an alert
questions.why: With a lengthy flight plan with several stops, a mishap on any leg probably means no one starts looking until 30 minutes after the ETA at the final destination, so the AIM says to file only to the first intended landing and refile for each leg [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]]. 1645 + 30 minutes = 1715; 1000 + 30 minutes = 1030; 1715 - 1030 = 6 hours 45 minutes. The 36 hours is the delay for pilots with no flight plan at all, while a filed plan is the most timely indicator that an aircraft is overdue [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]].

questions.q: Your learner plans to cross a mountain range in a light airplane at 9,500 ft, where the forecast wind is 32 knots. He says, 'That is under the AIM's 35 limit.' What do you teach?
options: He is right: the AIM limit is 35 knots, so 32 knots leaves a margin, and he can approach the passes low to stay under the strongest of the wind
The limit is 35 miles per hour, and 32 knots is about 37 mph, so not at that altitude; winds over the passes will be stronger still, and he needs gliding altitude in case the engine quits
The AIM limit is 35 miles per hour, but it applies only to the wind reported at the nearest airport, so the forecast at 9,500 ft does not count
The AIM limit is 35 miles per hour, and 32 knots is only about 28 mph, so the crossing is fine as long as he files a flight plan, follows well-known passes and keeps enough gliding altitude
questions.why: The AIM says not to fly a light aircraft when the winds aloft at your proposed altitude exceed 35 miles per hour, to expect much stronger winds over passes than reported a few miles away, and to approach passes with as much altitude as possible; the route should be over populated areas and well-known passes with enough altitude to glide to a safe landing if the engine fails, since flat fields are practically nonexistent [[34:162|AIM 7-6-7]]. 32 knots x 1.151 = 36.8 mph, above 35. Dividing instead of multiplying gives the wrong 28 mph.

questions.q: At night, your learner's parachute-equipped single loses its engine over unbroken forest; the airplane is still fully controllable. He asks, 'Does the AFH say this is a pull?' What is accurate?
options: Yes: the AFH lists an engine failure over terrain unsuitable for a forced landing as the first of its qualifying conditions for deploying the parachute

No: the AFH allows deployment only for pilot incapacitation, and any other use, an engine failure over a forest at night included, is outside the acceptable flight regime that the system was designed and certified for

Its examples are a catastrophic loss of controllability from a collision or mechanical failure, an actual loss of control, or pilot incapacitation; it does not settle this case, so the manufacturer's guidance decides
Yes, but only after a restart attempt at best glide, because the AFH puts the restart checklist ahead of deployment in every emergency
questions.why: The AFH gives a catastrophic loss of controllability due to a collision or mechanical failure, an actual loss of control, or pilot incapacitation as conditions that would qualify, says to deploy within an acceptable flight regime, and tells pilots to study and follow the guidance from the system's manufacturers and suppliers [[24:371|AFH 18-22]]. It does not say whether an engine failure over hostile terrain qualifies. Pilot incapacitation is when a passenger would generally deploy it, not the only trigger [[24:371|AFH 18-22]]. Settling the decision on the ground matters because the desire to save the airplane leads pilots to poor choices [[24:351|AFH 18-2]].

questions.q: A simulated forced landing ends in a firm real landing at the airport. Before shutdown your learner listens on 121.5 MHz, hears a swept tone, switches her ELT off, and the tone stops. She reaches to set it back to ARMED and go in. What do you teach?
options: Rearm it and go in: a short false alarm needs no report, because analog ELT signals on 121.5 MHz are no longer picked up by anyone after the satellites stopped
Leave it transmitting until a tower says it has heard the signal, because that confirms the ELT works, and only then switch it off and set it back to ARMED
Rearm it and test it at once with three audible sweeps, whatever the time, since a test right after a false alarm proves the unit is still serviceable
It was hers: maintenance might be needed before it goes back to ARMED, and she should tell the nearest air traffic facility about the inadvertent activation
questions.why: If an ELT signal is heard, turn off the aircraft's ELT to see if it is the source; if it was activated, maintenance might be required before it is returned to ARMED, and the pilot should notify the nearest air traffic facility of the inadvertent activation. Hard landings are a known cause, which is why the AIM wants 121.5 MHz monitored before engine shutdown [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]]. False alarms can interfere with real emergency transmissions and delay finding crash sites [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]]. Analog signals still reach nearby ATC facilities and overflying aircraft [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]], and analog tests belong in the first 5 minutes after the hour, three sweeps at most [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]].
